Bill.BriefDescription: Providing protections for juveniles in the custody of law enforcement officers.

BillBody.BillTitle: AN ACT Relating to juveniles in the custody of law enforcementofficers; adding a new section to chapter 13.40 RCW; and creating a newsection.
BillBody.EnactingClause: BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:

BillSection.RCWSLText: It is important for juveniles who are takeninto custody for questioning to understand their constitutional rightsto remain silent and to consult with a lawyer. They need to understandthe ramifications of choosing to speak with police. For this reason,the legislature finds that juveniles must be advised of their rights inageappropriate language. The legislature also finds that parents havean important interest in knowing if their children have been taken intopolice custody and where they are being held. The purpose of this actis to create a juvenile Miranda warning to be used to advise juvenilesof their rights before they are questioned in custody. The purpose ofthis act is also to require that law enforcement officers makereasonable efforts to notify parents, guardians, or custodians ofjuveniles taken into custody and where those juveniles are being held.

BegSecNew.BegSecText: A new section is added to chapter 13.40 RCWto read as follows:

BillSection.RCWSLText: (1) When a law enforcement officer takes a juvenile into custody,the officer must make a reasonable attempt to notify the juvenile'sparent, guardian, or custodian that the juvenile is in custody andwhere the juvenile is being held. (2) No statement, admission, or confession, written or oral, of ajuvenile under the age of eighteen given while in custody is admissibleunless, prior to taking of the statement, the juvenile is advised ofthe juvenile's rights in substantially the following manner: (a) You don't have to talk with us or answer our questions if youdon't want to. (b) If you decide to talk with us, you have to understand thatanything you say can be used against you. We can tell the probationofficer and the judge what you tell us. (c) You can talk to a lawyer now if you want to, and you can haveyour lawyer with you when we ask our questions. (d) If you want a lawyer, but you don't have enough money to hireyour own, the judge will get one for you and it won't cost youanything. (3) After a juvenile has been advised of his or her rights insubstantially the manner provided in this section, the law enforcementofficer shall ask the juvenile in substantially the following form: (a) Do you understand what I have said? (b) Do you want to ask me anything? (c) Do you want to talk with me now? (d) Do you want a lawyer, or not?
